screens.title: Administering Azure Database for MariaDB and Hyperscale (Citus)
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build practical skills for two Azure services that solve very different needs. First, you will learn how to administer Azure Database for MariaDB: provisioning servers, tuning key parameters, securing connections, and using Azure Monitor and automated backups to keep production systems healthy. Second, you'll explore Azure Database for PostgreSQL Hyperscale with the Citus extension. Hyperscale turns PostgreSQL into a distributed system by introducing a coordinator and worker nodes, and by distributing or replicating tables depending on workload. You'll see how the choice of distribution column controls query routing, colocation, and performance. Along the way we'll use concrete S Q L examples to create distributed and reference tables and explain common pitfalls such as data skew or choosing a distribution column that is not used by joins or filters. By the end of the chapter you'll know when to choose managed MariaDB and when Hyperscale (Citus) is the right pattern, how to provision and scale clusters, and how to design distributed tables for efficient queries.

Administering Azure Database for MariaDB and Hyperscale (Citus)

Understand managed MariaDB administration and how Hyperscale with Citus distributes PostgreSQL data for high throughput and massive scale.

In this lesson

You will learn provisioning, configuration, security, monitoring and backups for MariaDB, and the architecture, distribution strategies, and common operational tasks for Hyperscale (Citus).

Coming up

Guided SQL examples show how to create distributed and reference tables, and a hands-on activity walks through provisioning a Hyperscale cluster and distributing tables.

Topic: MariaDB Admin
Provision, tune parameters, secure access, and use Azure Monitor and automated backups to maintain operations.
Topic: Hyperscale (Citus)
Coordinator and worker nodes, distributed and reference tables, and distribution column design for scaling queries.
Topic: Hands-on
Provision a cluster, connect to the coordinator, create distributed and reference tables, then run queries to observe routing.
Visual concept
Cards show the two services and a simple relation: managed MariaDB for compatible web apps, Hyperscale (Citus) for sharded, high-volume workloads.
Quick example
Create a distributed table on the coordinator using a high-cardinality column like device_id, and create a reference lookup table for small frequently-joined data. This combination keeps joins efficient and enables parallel query execution.
Tip: When planning, list your most common query filters and joins. That list will guide whether MariaDB or Hyperscale (Citus) is a better fit, and which distribution column to choose for Citus.

screens.title: Azure Database for MariaDB — What and why
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Database for MariaDB is a fully managed relational database service based on the MariaDB community edition. As a managed offering it handles routine operations such as automated patching, backups, high availability, and the ability to choose compute and storage tiers. This makes it a straightforward choice when you are migrating or running applications that rely on the MySQL/MariaDB ecosystem. For example, a web application that currently runs on MySQL can often move to Azure Database for MariaDB and benefit from managed backups and a predictable operational model. A common misconception is that managed means you lose control. In reality you still manage server parameters and user roles; the platform removes undifferentiated heavy lifting like OS patching and storage replication. Practical admin tasks include provisioning a server, configuring parameters like max_connections, setting up firewall rules or Private Link for secure access, and monitoring resource usage in Azure Monitor. Key takeaway: treat MariaDB in Azure as a managed operational surface where platform services free you to focus on schema, queries, and capacity planning rather than infrastructure maintenance. Azure Database for MariaDB — What and why means azure database for mariadb is a managed mariadb service offering automation for maintenance while allowing parameter and user management.. In practical terms, managed mariadb for web-compatible workloads and familiar migrations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › MariaDB Overview
What is Azure Database for MariaDB?

A managed MariaDB server offering automated patching, backups, availability, and adjustable performance tiers. Admins keep control of parameters and security while Azure handles infrastructure tasks.

Typical administration tasks
  • Provision server with vCores, storage, and pricing tier.
  • Adjust server parameters like max_connections and query_cache_size.
  • Configure firewall rules, Virtual Network endpoints, or Private Link.
Concrete example

Migrate a MySQL-backed web app to Azure Database for MariaDB to use automated backups and managed patching while keeping the same client drivers and SQL dialect.

Key Takeaway

Use managed MariaDB when you need MySQL/MariaDB compatibility and want Azure to handle operational concerns while retaining control of schema and server parameters.

Misconception

Managed does not mean no control. Server parameters, users, and roles remain adjustable, but platform tasks like OS patching and automated backups are handled for you.

Why it matters

For small to medium transactional workloads, a managed MariaDB service reduces operational burden and simplifies migrations from existing MySQL environments.

Check your understanding: What admin action would you take first if CPU spikes are observed? (Answer: use Azure Monitor to inspect metrics, then review server parameters such as query_cache_size.)

screens.title: Provisioning and configuring MariaDB in Azure
screens.narratorSegment: Provisioning an Azure Database for MariaDB server is a repeatable process with a few choices that affect cost and performance. Start by selecting subscription and resource group, then choose a server name and administrator credentials. Next decide on compute and storage: pick vCores and storage size that match your workload profile. Finally choose a pricing tier and review networking options such as public access with firewall rules, Virtual Network service endpoints, or Private Link for private connectivity. After provisioning, configuration focuses on server parameters. Common parameters to inspect are max_connections to support concurrent clients and query_cache_size which can improve read performance but may cause C P U contention under heavy write workloads. A concrete workflow: provision a minimal server for testing, run a representative workload, monitor C P U and active connections with Azure Monitor, then adjust parameters incrementally and retest. A common mistake is changing many parameters at once; instead change one, measure, and revert if needed. This disciplined approach prevents configuration churn and helps you find the right balance between throughput and stability. Provisioning and configuring MariaDB in Azure means provision with appropriate vcores/storage and adjust server parameters carefully using monitoring to validate changes.. In practical terms, steps for creating a server and tuning key parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Provisioning MariaDB
Provisioning steps
  1. 1. Select subscription, resource group, server name, and admin credentials.
  2. 2. Choose compute (vCores) and storage capacity according to expected workload.
  3. 3. Configure network access: public IP with firewall rules or Private Link for private connectivity.
  4. 4. Review pricing tier and create the server; wait for the deployment to complete.
Practical tip

Start with a non-production test server to validate parameter changes under a representative workload before applying to production.

Configuring parameters
  • max_connections: increase to support more clients but monitor memory usage.
  • query_cache_size: may help reads but can cause CPU contention for high write workloads; test before enabling.
  • Other tuning: buffer sizes and thread settings based on workload profile.
Monitoring loop

Use Azure Monitor to track CPU, storage, and active connections. Change one parameter, run the workload, and observe metrics for stability and performance improvements.

Common mistake: changing many parameters at once. Fix: apply one change, measure, and then proceed to the next.

screens.title: Security and connectivity for MariaDB
screens.narratorSegment: Securing a managed MariaDB server in Azure involves two complementary layers: network-level controls and database-level authentication and authorization. At the network layer you can restrict access with firewall rules that allow specific client IP ranges. For stronger isolation, enable Virtual Network service endpoints or use Private Link so the database appears inside your private network. At the database layer you manage users, roles, and permissions to ensure least-privilege access to schemas and objects. A concrete example: a web application tier in an Azure virtual network should access the MariaDB server via Private Link so traffic does not traverse the public internet, and the application should connect using a dedicated database user with only the required privileges. A common misconception is that firewall rules alone are sufficient; they protect network access but do not replace proper database user management or encryption. Also verify TLS is enforced for connections and rotate admin credentials according to your security policy. Regularly audit logins and failed attempts through diagnostic logs and Azure Monitor to detect anomalous behavior. The goal is a layered defense that combines network isolation, encrypted transport, and tight database permissions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Security & Connectivity
Network controls
  • Firewall rules: restrict by client IP ranges.
  • Virtual Network service endpoints: narrow access to VNets.
  • Private Link: allow private connectivity without public endpoints.
Database access

Manage users and roles, enforce least privilege, and use TLS for encrypted transport. Rotate admin credentials and audit access regularly.

Concrete scenario

Place an app tier in a VNet and connect via Private Link. Create an application user with minimal privileges for data operations; reserve the admin account for maintenance.

Common mistake

Relying solely on firewall rules. Fix by combining network isolation with user privilege controls and enforced TLS.

screens.title: Monitoring, backups, and recovery for MariaDB
screens.narratorSegment: Operational resilience includes monitoring resource health and having a recovery plan. Use Azure Monitor to track C P U utilization, storage usage, and active connections for your MariaDB server. Set alerts on thresholds that matter for your application, such as C P U above a sustained percentage or storage approaching capacity. Azure Database for MariaDB also provides automated backups with point-in-time restore; know your retention window and test restores periodically. A concrete workflow: enable diagnostic settings to send logs and metrics to a Log Analytics workspace, create alert rules for key metrics, and run a scheduled test of point-in-time restore into a non-production environment to verify backup integrity. A common misconception is that backups are only for disaster recovery; they are also useful for data migration and point-in-time debugging. Also monitor for long-running queries and use performance insights where available. Document your recovery runbook: steps to scale compute, restore from backup, and redirect application connections. Regular testing closes the loop between monitoring, alerting, and recovery readiness. Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Monitoring & Backups
Key metrics to monitor
  • CPU utilization and sustained spikes.
  • Storage consumption and I/O latency.
  • Active connections and long-running queries.
Backup and restore

Azure provides automated backups and point-in-time restore. Understand retention settings and validate restores by performing periodic recovery drills into a test server.

Concrete example

Send diagnostic logs to Log Analytics, create an alert for sustained CPU > 80%, and have a runbook that scales up compute and notifies the on-call DBA while performing a backup validation into staging.

Key Takeaway

Monitoring plus routine restore tests ensure that backups are usable and recovery procedures are reliable when needed.

screens.title: Hyperscale (Citus) — architecture and core concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Hyperscale (Citus) transforms PostgreSQL into a distributed database by introducing two logical roles: a coordinator node and multiple worker nodes. The coordinator is the entry point for applications: it stores metadata about distributed tables and routes queries to the appropriate worker nodes. Worker nodes each store shards of distributed tables and execute query fragments in parallel. Conceptually, when you distribute a table, the rows are partitioned across worker nodes based on a distribution column; the coordinator keeps the mapping and plans queries so they run where data lives. Reference tables are replicated on each worker and are ideal for small lookup data that is frequently joined; local tables remain on the coordinator and are used for small administrative datasets. The benefit of this model is horizontal scaling: by adding worker nodes you increase storage and parallel processing capacity. A common misconception is that Hyperscale eliminates the need for schema design; in fact, choosing which tables to distribute or replicate and selecting the distribution column remains a critical design task. Key takeaway: Citus gives PostgreSQL horizontal scale, but you must design distribution deliberately to get the expected performance gains.

keyIdea.text: Coordinator routes queries and stores metadata; worker nodes hold shards and perform parallel execution on distributed tables.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Hyperscale Architecture
Coordinator and workers
Coordinator node

Entry point for applications; holds metadata about shard placement and rewrites queries to run across worker nodes.

Worker nodes

Store shards of distributed tables and execute query fragments in parallel to scale storage and CPU capacity horizontally.

Table types
  • Distributed tables: sharded by a distribution column across workers.
  • Reference tables: fully replicated on each worker, good for small lookup data.
  • Local tables: stored only on the coordinator for small admin data.
Misconception check

Citus makes scaling easier but does not remove the need for thoughtful schema and distribution design; poor choices can cause data movement and slow queries.

screens.title: Distributed, reference, and local tables
screens.narratorSegment: Citus supports three table placement strategies and choosing among them affects performance and storage. Distributed tables are sharded across worker nodes using a distribution column; they are the primary mechanism for scaling large datasets. Use distributed tables when a table contains many rows and queries commonly filter or join on the distribution column. Reference tables are small tables that are fully replicated to every worker; these are great for lookup data or small dimension tables that are frequently joined with a distributed table. Local tables live only on the coordinator and are used for small administrative or control data that does not benefit from distribution. Consider a concrete example: an orders table with millions of rows should be distributed by customer_id if queries often aggregate or filter by customer. A customers lookup with a few thousand rows should be a reference table to avoid remote joins. A common mistake is selecting a low-cardinality distribution column, which leads to skew—some workers receive more data than others and performance degrades. Always evaluate cardinality and query patterns before choosing the distribution column. Key takeaway: proper use of distributed and reference tables enables colocated joins and efficient parallel execution.

keyIdea.title: Table placement rules
keyIdea.text: Distribute large, frequently-filtered tables; replicate small lookup tables as reference; keep small admin data local to the coordinator.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Table Placement
Distributed tables

Sharded by a distribution column across workers. Best for large tables where queries filter or join on the distribution column.

Reference tables

Replicated on all workers. Ideal for small lookup tables that are frequently joined with distributed tables without changing often.

Local tables

Stored on the coordinator only. Use for small administrative data that doesn't need to be distributed.

Concrete SQL example
-- Create a distributed table
CREATE TABLE products (
  product_id INT,
  product_name TEXT,
  category_id INT,
  price DECIMAL
);
SELECT create_distributed_table('products', 'category_id');

-- Create a reference table
CREATE TABLE categories (
  category_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  category_name TEXT
);
SELECT create_reference_table('categories');
Common mistake

Choosing a low-cardinality distribution column. Fix: pick a high-cardinality column that is used by filters and joins to enable colocation and even shard distribution.

screens.title: Provision, connect, and create distributed tables (hands-on)
screens.narratorSegment: This slide walks through the hands-on sequence to provision a Hyperscale (Citus) cluster, connect to the coordinator, and create distributed and reference tables using S Q L. In the Azure portal choose Create for Azure Database for PostgreSQL, select Hyperscale (Citus) server group, provide subscription, resource group, and a unique server group name. Choose coordinator and worker compute and storage sizes and add at least two worker nodes for demonstration. After deployment, copy the psql connection string for the coordinator and open your terminal. A safe command shows the pattern for creating a distributed table: first define the table schema, then call create_distributed_table specifying the distribution column. For smaller lookup tables use create_reference_table to replicate data to all workers. For example, create a products table and distribute by category_id, and create a categories reference table so joins on category_id are colocated and efficient. Provision and connect

SQL example (run on coordinator)

  product_name TEXT,

);

screens.title: Query behavior and performance considerations in Citus
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding how queries run in a Hyperscale (Citus) cluster helps you design schemas that avoid cross-node data movement. When a query includes the distribution column in its WHERE clause or JOIN conditions, the coordinator can route the query directly to the worker where the relevant shard lives, enabling single-node execution or efficient parallel aggregation. For joins between two distributed tables, performance is best when both tables share the same distribution column and values are colocated on the same workers. If queries do not use the distribution column or if distributions differ, the coordinator may need to move data between workers or perform a coordinator-side join, which is less efficient. A concrete example: if orders are distributed by customer_id and you frequently join orders with order_items on order_id but order_items are distributed by product_id, joins will require data movement. A common mistake is not checking cardinality: a distribution column with skew (many rows mapping to a few shard keys) results in hotspots. To validate query behavior, run explain plans and check how many worker nodes are involved. Key takeaway: design distribution to match your most common filters and joins to minimize cross-node data movement and maximize parallel processing.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Query Behavior
How routing works

If a query filters or joins on the distribution column, the coordinator routes the work to the relevant worker(s), enabling localized execution and efficient parallelism.

Colocation for joins

For joins between distributed tables, colocate them by using the same distribution column so the join can execute on workers without moving data across nodes.

Failure modes and fixes
  • Data skew: rebalance by choosing a different distribution column or pre-hashing keys.
  • Cross-node joins: refactor schema to use reference tables or align distribution keys.
  • Lack of distribution column in queries: encourage application queries to filter by the distribution key for performance.
Check with EXPLAIN

Run explain plans on the coordinator to see if queries are routed to workers and how many nodes participate. This reveals whether your distribution choices are effective.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build practical skills for two Azure services that solve very different needs. First, you will learn how to administer Azure Database for MariaDB: provisioning servers, tuning key parameters, securing connections, and using Azure Monitor and automated backups to keep production systems healthy. Second, you'll explore Azure Database for PostgreSQL Hyperscale with the Citus extension. Hyperscale turns PostgreSQL into a distributed system by introducing a coordinator and worker nodes, and by distributing or replicating tables depending on workload. You'll see how the choice of distribution column controls query routing, colocation, and performance. Along the way we'll use concrete S Q L examples to create distributed and reference tables and explain common pitfalls such as data skew or choosing a distribution column that is not used by joins or filters. By the end of the chapter you'll know when to choose managed MariaDB and when Hyperscale (Citus) is the right pattern, how to provision and scale clusters, and how to design distributed tables for efficient queries.

By the end of this chapter you will have four concrete, verifiable skills. First, you will be able to provision and perform routine administration for Azure Database for MariaDB, including selecting compute and storage tiers and applying server parameters for workload tuning. Second, you will understand the architecture of Hyperscale (Citus): the roles of coordinator and worker nodes, and why sharding enables horizontal scaling for large datasets. Third, you will be able to provision and scale a Hyperscale cluster, add or remove worker nodes, and connect to the coordinator for management. Fourth, you will know how to design distributed tables, choose a distribution column with high cardinality and join relevance, and create reference and local tables to keep joins efficient. Each objective focuses on a practical task you can demonstrate, and each maps to management actions you'll perform in the portal or via psql on the coordinator. These skills make you ready to manage both small-to-medium transactional workloads on MariaDB and large-scale analytical or high-throughput workloads on Hyperscale (Citus).

These objectives map to specific practical tasks you'll perform. You will provision a MariaDB server and show how to change a server parameter safely, using a small performance test to observe impact. You will provision a Hyperscale (Citus) server group with at least two worker nodes, connect to the coordinator with psql, and execute S Q L commands to create distributed and reference tables. You will insert sample rows and run queries that filter on the distribution column to observe efficient routing, and you will run joins with a replicated reference table to see how colocation avoids data movement. Finally, you will use Azure Monitor metrics and the platform backup features to demonstrate a point-in-time restore on MariaDB. Each task is something you can show as evidence of competency and ties directly to administrative responsibilities in production environments.

Azure Database for MariaDB is a fully managed relational database service based on the MariaDB community edition. As a managed offering it handles routine operations such as automated patching, backups, high availability, and the ability to choose compute and storage tiers. This makes it a straightforward choice when you are migrating or running applications that rely on the MySQL/MariaDB ecosystem. For example, a web application that currently runs on MySQL can often move to Azure Database for MariaDB and benefit from managed backups and a predictable operational model. A common misconception is that managed means you lose control. In reality you still manage server parameters and user roles; the platform removes undifferentiated heavy lifting like OS patching and storage replication. Practical admin tasks include provisioning a server, configuring parameters like max_connections, setting up firewall rules or Private Link for secure access, and monitoring resource usage in Azure Monitor. Key takeaway: treat MariaDB in Azure as a managed operational surface where platform services free you to focus on schema, queries, and capacity planning rather than infrastructure maintenance. Azure Database for MariaDB — What and why means azure database for mariadb is a managed mariadb service offering automation for maintenance while allowing parameter and user management.. In practical terms, managed mariadb for web-compatible workloads and familiar migrations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Provisioning an Azure Database for MariaDB server is a repeatable process with a few choices that affect cost and performance. Start by selecting subscription and resource group, then choose a server name and administrator credentials. Next decide on compute and storage: pick vCores and storage size that match your workload profile. Finally choose a pricing tier and review networking options such as public access with firewall rules, Virtual Network service endpoints, or Private Link for private connectivity. After provisioning, configuration focuses on server parameters. Common parameters to inspect are max_connections to support concurrent clients and query_cache_size which can improve read performance but may cause C P U contention under heavy write workloads. A concrete workflow: provision a minimal server for testing, run a representative workload, monitor C P U and active connections with Azure Monitor, then adjust parameters incrementally and retest. A common mistake is changing many parameters at once; instead change one, measure, and revert if needed. This disciplined approach prevents configuration churn and helps you find the right balance between throughput and stability. Securing a managed MariaDB server in Azure involves two complementary layers: network-level controls and database-level authentication and authorization. At the network layer you can restrict access with firewall rules that allow specific client IP ranges. For stronger isolation, enable Virtual Network service endpoints or use Private Link so the database appears inside your private network. At the database layer you manage users, roles, and permissions to ensure least-privilege access to schemas and objects. A concrete example: a web application tier in an Azure virtual network should access the MariaDB server via Private Link so traffic does not traverse the public internet, and the application should connect using a dedicated database user with only the required privileges. A common misconception is that firewall rules alone are sufficient; they protect network access but do not replace proper database user management or encryption. Also verify TLS is enforced for connections and rotate admin credentials according to your security policy. Regularly audit logins and failed attempts through diagnostic logs and Azure Monitor to detect anomalous behavior. The goal is a layered defense that combines network isolation, encrypted transport, and tight database permissions.

Operational resilience includes monitoring resource health and having a recovery plan. Use Azure Monitor to track C P U utilization, storage usage, and active connections for your MariaDB server. Set alerts on thresholds that matter for your application, such as C P U above a sustained percentage or storage approaching capacity. Azure Database for MariaDB also provides automated backups with point-in-time restore; know your retention window and test restores periodically. A concrete workflow: enable diagnostic settings to send logs and metrics to a Log Analytics workspace, create alert rules for key metrics, and run a scheduled test of point-in-time restore into a non-production environment to verify backup integrity. A common misconception is that backups are only for disaster recovery; they are also useful for data migration and point-in-time debugging. Also monitor for long-running queries and use performance insights where available. Document your recovery runbook: steps to scale compute, restore from backup, and redirect application connections. Regular testing closes the loop between monitoring, alerting, and recovery readiness. Monitoring, backups, and recovery for MariaDB means monitor key metrics, set alerts, understand backup retention, and regularly test point-in-time restores as part of your recovery plan.. Hyperscale (Citus) transforms PostgreSQL into a distributed database by introducing two logical roles: a coordinator node and multiple worker nodes. The coordinator is the entry point for applications: it stores metadata about distributed tables and routes queries to the appropriate worker nodes. Worker nodes each store shards of distributed tables and execute query fragments in parallel. Conceptually, when you distribute a table, the rows are partitioned across worker nodes based on a distribution column; the coordinator keeps the mapping and plans queries so they run where data lives. Reference tables are replicated on each worker and are ideal for small lookup data that is frequently joined; local tables remain on the coordinator and are used for small administrative datasets. The benefit of this model is horizontal scaling: by adding worker nodes you increase storage and parallel processing capacity. A common misconception is that Hyperscale eliminates the need for schema design; in fact, choosing which tables to distribute or replicate and selecting the distribution column remains a critical design task. Key takeaway: Citus gives PostgreSQL horizontal scale, but you must design distribution deliberately to get the expected performance gains.

Citus supports three table placement strategies and choosing among them affects performance and storage. Distributed tables are sharded across worker nodes using a distribution column; they are the primary mechanism for scaling large datasets. Use distributed tables when a table contains many rows and queries commonly filter or join on the distribution column. Reference tables are small tables that are fully replicated to every worker; these are great for lookup data or small dimension tables that are frequently joined with a distributed table. Local tables live only on the coordinator and are used for small administrative or control data that does not benefit from distribution. Consider a concrete example: an orders table with millions of rows should be distributed by customer_id if queries often aggregate or filter by customer. A customers lookup with a few thousand rows should be a reference table to avoid remote joins. A common mistake is selecting a low-cardinality distribution column, which leads to skew—some workers receive more data than others and performance degrades. Always evaluate cardinality and query patterns before choosing the distribution column. Key takeaway: proper use of distributed and reference tables enables colocated joins and efficient parallel execution.
